description_en: Bistabara Stone Memorial Pillars, located near a free-standingśikharatemple (JUM0454) in the northern end of the village of Bistabara, date from the 13th-16th centuries. A newly laid cement path leads to the site, which is now part of a walled complex built by the village committee. The complex includes a new single-story concrete structure that will serve as a small museum. To the north is a cluster of threeśikharatemples (JUM0450,JUM0451andJUM0452).Pillar 001 (JUM0455-001) is located to the east of theśikharatemple, just above the cement path, on the edge of a terraced field. This is most likely the most ornately ornamented pillar in west Nepal. The carved side is oriented eastward. Three lines of eroded inscription in Nāgarī script can be found in the lower register. Above it is a pair of spirals in dotted circles, followed by two crosses, a large central motif of spiralled pike, a pair of four-branched stars, a rosette and two top spirals.Pillar 002 (JUM0455-002) is located 10 meters north of theśikharatemple, on the left side of the cement path. The carved side is oriented to eastward. Because it is heavily eroded, only a portion of the lower register is discernible. It has a shallow carved representation of a stepped monument topped with a pike. The stepped monument could be astūpa, indicating that it was erected by Buddhists.Pillar 003 (JUM0455-003) is laying on the ground, one meter west of theśikharatemple. It is damaged. The carving on its remaining part includes a large rosette, two spirals and a losange with a spiral inside.From the 13th to the 16th centuries, such stone memorial pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin. They are erected to honour the memory of deceased people, most of whom were warriors (Andolfatto 2019). In Bistabara, there are no inscriptions on the pillars (or any discernible ones). Their typology, as well as the nearby presence of a pillar dated 1500 CE, suggests that they were built between the 13th and 16th centuries.
references: REFERENCES Andolfatto, David C. 2019. Le Pays aux Cent-Vingt-Cinq-Mille Montagnes. Etude Archéologique du Bassin de la Karnali (Népal) entre le XIIe et le XVIe siècle . Paris: Sorbonne Université.
